title: 'Address already in use' is a distinct diagnosis from a bad config
explanation: nginx logging `Address already in use` on startup means the kernel refused to let it bind the socket because something else already holds it — this is a fact about port ownership, not about anything in nginx's own config files. Reaching for `nginx -t` or re-checking the config here would be looking in the wrong place entirely.

title: Find out who actually owns the port
explanation: `sudo ss -tlnp | grep 8080` (or `sudo lsof -i :8080`) names the real occupant directly, by process name and PID — no guessing required. Here it's `legacy-agent`, a process with no obvious connection to the web app at all.

title: Understand why a decommissioned process is still running
explanation: `legacy-agent` was supposed to be retired months ago, but its startup entry was never cleaned up, so it still launches on every boot — and because it starts before nginx does, it wins the race for port 8080 first, every single time. nginx isn't misconfigured; it's simply losing a startup race for a socket it should own uncontested.

title: Kill precisely the right process
explanation: `pkill -x legacy-agent` matches the exact process name rather than doing a substring match against the full command line (`-f`), which matters here because the container's own startup command happens to mention that same path as plain text — a `-f` match could catch more than intended. Re-checking `ss -tlnp | grep 8080` confirms the port is genuinely free before starting anything new.

title: Start the real service only once the port is clear
explanation: `sudo service nginx start` now succeeds because nothing is contesting the socket, and `curl http://localhost:8080/` reaching the app confirms the right process — not just *a* process — is finally the one holding port 8080.
